01 · TEXAS TAX Receipt discrepancy

Displayed tax rate does not match the math

Receipt 00BMI-001 says 6.25%, but $22.25 on $445.00 equals 5.00%. If Texas short-term rental tax applies, 10% of $445.00 would be $44.50. ZEVO still needs to explain what tax it charged, who was responsible for it, and whether it was actually paid to Texas.

02 · CHARGE & REFUND Disputed

Recovery fees and refunds still need proof

ZEVO added $275.73 in recovery and recharge fees after the booking was canceled. ZEVO also shows $389.43 in refunds, but the available records do not prove that money actually reached the card. ZEVO should explain the pickup instruction, the rule used to charge the fees, and provide bank or payment-company proof of the refunds.

Not finding a Form D in a public name search does not, by itself, prove a violation.

These are questions that still need records and explanations. They are not final legal conclusions. The six original findings and supporting evidence remain available for reference.

COMPLIANCE QUESTIONSWhat the records raise · what ZEVO still needs to prove
01 / STATE · TEXASNeeds records

What tax was charged, and was it paid correctly?

What the records show: the receipt labels $22.25 as “6.25%” tax on $445.00, but the math equals 5.00%. Texas generally uses a 10% state rate for taxable 1–30 day vehicle rentals, which would be $44.50 on $445.00. Public Texas Comptroller searches under the company name and taxpayer number reviewed did not locate a matching tax account, but that does not prove no account exists under another responsible party or name.

Why it matters: the dollar difference on one receipt is small by itself. The bigger question is whether the same billing setup produced the same mismatch on other rentals. If the printed percentage and the calculated percentage came from the same system rule, the error could repeat across many transactions. ZEVO should show whether this was a one-time manual mistake or a billing-system problem, in addition to explaining who was responsible for the tax and whether it was paid correctly.

What ZEVO should provide: the rental agreement, vehicle-owner agreement, the Texas tax account used, the tax return, proof of payment, and an explanation of how the tax amount was calculated.

Texas Tax Code §§152.026, 152.045 · Comptroller · Peer-to-peer guidance
02 / STATE · TEXASConsumer dispute

Why was a company-directed pickup called abandonment?

What the records show: after the booking was canceled and pickup was directed, ZEVO recorded a $245.73 recovery fee and a $30 recharge fee as customer “abandonment.” A $245.73 tow invoice shows that a tow cost existed, but it does not prove the customer was responsible for paying it.

Why it matters: if ZEVO charged a customer for a fee its own policy did not allow, or described the transaction in a misleading way, that could create consumer-protection and refund issues. Whether any law was actually violated depends on the full facts.

What ZEVO should provide: the policy in effect that day, cancellation and pickup messages, tow request, battery/recharge records, fee approval, and proof of what money was actually collected or refunded.

Texas Business & Commerce Code §§17.46, 17.50 · Texas law
03 / FEDERALConditional

Billing and background-screening questions

Questions to answer: Did ZEVO give inaccurate information about fees or refunds? Did a Checkr consumer report play any part in canceling the booking? If it did, was the customer given any notice required by law?

Why it matters: federal consumer-protection rules may apply if misleading billing occurred. Fair Credit Reporting Act duties may also apply if a consumer report was actually used to make the cancellation decision. The current record is not enough to say that those duties were triggered.

What ZEVO should provide: the actual Checkr report, the reason for the cancellation, any notices sent to the customer, and the original support and cancellation records.

FTC Act · FCRA
04 / SECURITIES · SECRecords still needed

Fundraising and Form D records

What the records show: public searches under the ZEVO names reviewed did not locate a matching Form D. That search result alone does not tell us whether a Form D was required, which company sold the investment, or when the first investor committed.

Why it matters: for fundraising rounds that rely on Regulation D, the SEC generally requires a Form D within 15 calendar days after the first sale. A late or missing Form D can create compliance and investor-review questions, although it does not automatically eliminate the Regulation D exemption.

What ZEVO should provide: the legal name and SEC ID (CIK) of each company that raised money, the investment agreements, first investor date, rule or exemption used, Form D links or filing numbers, state filings, and investor communications.

Regulation D Rules 503, 506, 507 · SEC Form D FAQ
HOW THESE ISSUES COULD AFFECT ZEVO'S BUSINESS RECORDSQuestions to verify · not proven errors
R01

How much of each rental should ZEVO count as money it actually earned?

ZEVO should show whether it provides the rental itself or mainly connects customers with vehicle hosts. That affects whether the company should treat the full rental price as money it earned or only the fee it keeps. A large total value of bookings is not automatically the same as company revenue.

FINANCIAL RECORDS
R02

Are taxes kept separate from money ZEVO earns?

Money collected for taxes generally should be tracked separately from money the company earns. ZEVO should show where the tax from this rental was recorded and whether it was paid to the correct government account. If tax money was treated as company income, the company could appear to have earned more than it actually did while also understating taxes still owed.

FINANCIAL RECORDS
R03

Did the refunds actually reach the customer's card?

ZEVO shows $389.43 in refunds, but a screen saying “Paid” is not enough to prove the cardholder received the money. ZEVO should provide the refund IDs from ZEVO's payment company, bank tracking numbers (ARNs), and confirmation from the card company showing where each refund ended up.

REFUNDS
R04

What do the $275.73 fees and the extra $2.09 represent?

ZEVO should explain the $275.73 in later recovery and recharge fees and the separate $2.09 shown in the records. The key question is whether each amount had a valid reason, was actually charged or collected, and was recorded consistently with the cancellation and refund history.

FINANCIAL RECORDS
R05

Can ZEVO connect investor money to the investments it actually issued?

ZEVO should be able to match money received from investors to the shares, notes, or other investments it actually issued. Investor materials should also agree with the company's official financial records. Not finding a Form D by itself does not prove those records are wrong.

FUNDRAISING
IF THE RECORDS CONFIRM PROBLEMS

Potential consequences

Possible outcomes could include customer refunds, corrected tax filings, interest or penalties, changes to ZEVO's financial records, more questions from investors or lenders, or review by a regulator. Which outcomes apply depends on what the missing records ultimately show.

For professional reviewers, the underlying accounting and legal references are preserved here: How company revenue should be recorded · When a platform records the full price versus only its fee. This review uses the receipts, support messages, taxpayer-search screenshots, and research currently available. Customer reviews are third-party claims and are not treated as proven facts. ZEVO's internal accounting records, tax returns, and investor transaction records have not been provided.

Receipt 00BMI-001 says the tax rate was 6.25%, but $22.25 on $445.00 equals 5.00%. ZEVO needs to explain what type of tax this was, how long the rental agreement lasted, what amount was taxed, who was responsible for the tax, and whether it was paid.

GUIDED EVIDENCE REVIEW0 answers recorded

What tax was charged —
and what should it have been?

Receipt 00BMI-001 says 6.25%, but $22.25 on $445.00 is 5.00%. Texas generally uses a 10% state rate for taxable vehicle rentals of 30 days or less. The remaining questions are simple: what tax was this, how long was the rental agreement, what amount was taxed, who owed the tax to Texas, and was it actually paid?

Texas rule in plain English. Texas generally charges 10% state rental tax on taxable vehicle-rental contracts of 30 days or less and 6.25% on contracts from 31 through 180 days. In a peer-to-peer rental, the vehicle owner may be the party responsible for the tax rather than the platform. ZEVO should identify who was responsible here. Exemptions, local taxes, and the correct amount being taxed can change the final result. Official rates ↗ · Peer-to-peer Comptroller guidance ↗

REQUESTED RESOLUTION

Full refund and reversal of disputed fees

I dispute ZEVO's decision to call this pickup customer abandonment. ZEVO canceled the booking after pickup and told me to leave the vehicle for retrieval. I am requesting a full refund of the original $667.25 payment, reversal of the $275.73 in recovery and recharge fees, repayment of any part of those fees that was collected, and proof showing where every claimed refund actually went. Only refunds proven to have reached my card should reduce the amount still owed. Please identify the policy rule and records supporting any amount ZEVO refuses to return.

ZEVO's published Terms of Service address improper returns, recovery fees and guest cancellation. The evidence record describes a ZEVO-initiated cancellation, not a guest cancellation.
WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE BUSINESSUnsupported fees and unproven refunds can distort the company's records

ZEVO should be able to show why the $275.73 fee was valid, whether it was actually collected, and where it was recorded. It should also prove that the $389.43 in claimed refunds reached the customer before treating those refunds as complete. The separate $2.09 shown in the records also needs a simple explanation.

CURRENT TAKEAWAY

What can be concluded today?

A tow invoice can prove that a tow cost existed, but it does not prove the customer owed it. ZEVO still needs to show why the pickup was called abandonment, why each fee was allowed, and whether the refunds actually reached the card.

THE BASIC RULEA Form D is required for many Regulation D fundraising rounds, but not for every way a company can legally raise money.

For fundraising that relies on Regulation D Rule 504 or 506, or Section 4(a)(5), the SEC generally requires Form D within 15 calendar days after the first investor is legally committed. A late or missing filing does not automatically eliminate the exemption.
